scenes.title: Dynamic DAGs & Task Mapping
scenes.narration: This lesson explores how Airflow builds pipelines whose shape is not fully known until runtime, using dynamic task mapping.

scenes.title: The problem with fixed DAGs
bullets: Task count is often unknown when writing code
Files, partitions, or tables vary each run
Hard-coding one task per item does not scale
scenes.narration: A static DAG assumes you know every task at authoring time, but reality is messier. The number of files to process, partitions to load, or tables to sync often changes from run to run. Hard-coding one task per item is brittle and cannot adapt, which is exactly the gap that dynamic task mapping fills.

scenes.title: Two kinds of dynamism

left.heading: Dynamic DAG generation
points: Loop over config to create many DAGs or tasks

right.heading: Dynamic task mapping
points: Fan out one task over a runtime list

scenes.narration: There are two distinct techniques. Dynamic DAG generation loops over some configuration to programmatically create many tasks or even many DAGs, and this happens at parse time when the file is read. Dynamic task mapping is different: it fans a single task out over a list that is only known at run time, using Airflow's native expand API. The distinction matters because parse-time and run-time dynamism behave very differently.

scenes.title: Dynamic task mapping with expand
scenes.narration: This example shows task mapping in action. The list_files task returns a list that is only computed when the DAG runs. Calling expand on the process task tells Airflow to create one mapped instance of process for each element of that list. So a three-file run produces three parallel process tasks, while a ten-file run produces ten, all without changing the code. The number of tasks adapts to the data automatically.

scenes.title: How mapping executes
steps: Scheduler expands into N mapped instances
Instances run in parallel, then collapse
scenes.narration: At execution the upstream task produces its list, and the scheduler expands the mapped task into as many instances as there are items. Those instances run in parallel, subject to your concurrency limits, and their results can then be collapsed back together for a downstream task to consume. This gives you elastic parallelism that scales precisely with the data at hand.

scenes.text: Prefer native task mapping over hand-rolled loops for runtime fan-out, and cap parallelism so a huge list cannot overwhelm your workers.
scenes.narration: The recommendation is to prefer native task mapping over hand-rolled loops whenever the fan-out depends on runtime data, and to cap the parallelism so that an unexpectedly huge list cannot overwhelm your workers all at once.
